screens.title: Understanding Inheritance: The extends Keyword
screens.subtitle: How Java reuses behavior and builds clear superclass–subclass relationships

narration.text: In this lesson we'll explore inheritance in Java and why the extends keyword matters. Inheritance lets one class acquire fields and methods from another, reducing duplication and giving classes a clear "is-a" relationship. For example, a Car is a Vehicle and can reuse speed, brand, and start behavior defined once in Vehicle. You will learn how to declare a subclass with extends, how constructors and the super keyword connect object initialization across classes, and how overriding changes behavior while keeping a shared interface. We will also cover access rules — why private members are hidden, how protected provides a middle ground, and when to use public interfaces. Throughout, concrete examples like Vehicle→Car and a Shape→Circle/Rectangle activity will show how to design and test these relationships. By the end of this chapter you should be able to decide when to extract a superclass, write a subclass that reuses functionality, and avoid common pitfalls such as forgetting to call a necessary superclass constructor. Think about a hierarchy you use in everyday code: what shared behavior would you factor into a superclass, and what belongs only in specific subclasses?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Inheritance enables code reuse and models "is-a" relationships; extends declares that relationship in Java.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Understanding Inheritance
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Understanding Inheritance

Learn how extends forms superclass–subclass links, how constructors and super connect initialization, and how overriding customizes behavior.

In this lesson

You will see a Vehicle → Car example, learn to use extends and super, and practice a Shape hierarchy that overrides calculateArea.

Why it matters

Inheritance reduces duplicate code and provides a clear place to change behavior shared across types. It keeps designs maintainable when used carefully.

Explore Key Topics
extends

Declares the subclass relationship so members are inherited.

super

Connects constructors and accesses the superclass implementation.

Overriding

Replace inherited behavior while preserving the method signature.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives guide our practice and checks. First, you will define inheritance and explain its purpose in object-oriented design: that means being able to describe how a subclass reuses fields and methods of a superclass and why that reduces duplication. Second, you will demonstrate the use of the extends keyword: you will write a subclass declaration that correctly inherits a superclass and compile a small example that calls inherited methods. Third, you'll differentiate overriding from overloading and apply the @Override annotation so the compiler helps you detect signature mistakes. Finally on this screen you will learn to use super to call either a superclass constructor or a superclass method. Each objective pairs a declarative skill with a simple coding check so you can verify competency. For example, you might write a Car that extends Vehicle and use super(brand) in Car’s constructor; that confirms you understand both extends and super. A common misconception is thinking private members can be overridden — we will be explicit about access rules so you don’t repeat that error. These competencies form the baseline for safe, reusable class hierarchies.

keyIdea.title: Learning focus
keyIdea.text: Define, use, and reason about inheritance, extends, overriding, @Override, and super.

screens.title: What is Inheritance in Java?
screens.subtitle: A precise definition and practical purpose

narration.text: Inheritance is a mechanism where one class acquires fields and methods from another class. It formalizes a reuse relationship so you can place shared state and behavior in one location, the superclass, and let multiple subclasses inherit those members. Practically, inheritance reduces repetition: if Vehicle defines brand, speed, and start, Car and Motorcycle reuse those members rather than declaring them again. This also creates a logical "is-a" relationship: a Car is a Vehicle, which clarifies intent and enables polymorphism later on. A concrete example is the Vehicle class with a start method; neither Car nor Motorcycle needs its own start implementation unless they require special behavior. A common misconception is thinking inheritance is just for code reuse; in fact, it also encodes conceptual relationships and should be used when a true subtype relationship exists. Another confusion is believing inheritance substitutes composition in every case — composition is often a better choice when the relationship is "has-a" rather than "is-a." Key takeaway: use inheritance to model genuine subclass relationships and centralize common behavior. Can you name a group of related types in your code where a shared superclass would simplify maintenance?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse members of a superclass and expresses an "is-a" relationship in code.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is Inheritance in Java?
Definition

Inheritance explained

Inheritance allows one class to acquire properties and behaviors from another class to promote reuse and express subtype relationships.

• Reuse common fields and methods defined in a superclass.
• Model a natural "is-a" relationship, enabling clearer design intent.
• Avoid duplicating logic across multiple related classes.
Key Takeaway

Choose inheritance when subclasses truly are specialized forms of a superclass, not merely to copy code.

Example

Vehicle has brand, speed, and start(); Car and Motorcycle automatically inherit these members and share behavior unless overridden.

Analogy and structure
Analogy

Think of a blueprint for Vehicle and individual house models that inherit the blueprint's rooms and plumbing. Subclasses add or change specifics.

Misconception

Inheritance is not a free-for-all for reuse; it should model a genuine subtype relationship rather than just share code.

Check your understanding

Name a pair of classes in your projects that could form a true "is-a" relationship and explain what would belong in the superclass.

screens.title: Using the extends Keyword
screens.subtitle: Declare a subclass and inherit members from the superclass

narration.text: The extends keyword establishes the inheritance link in Java. When you write class Car extends Vehicle, Car becomes a subclass that inherits all non-private fields and methods of Vehicle. This makes Car objects able to call inherited methods like start or accelerate without redefining them. A simple, concrete example from the chapter shows Vehicle with brand, speed, and start(), and Car extends Vehicle adding numberOfDoors and honk(). In code, Car's constructor calls super(brand) to initialize the Vehicle portion of the object. Pay attention to two practical points: first, subclass constructors must either call a superclass constructor explicitly or rely on the implicit no-argument super() call; if the superclass lacks a no-argument constructor, you must call its parameterized constructor. Second, inheritance does not grant access to private members; private fields are inherited but inaccessible directly by the subclass. A common error is forgetting to invoke super(...) when required and observing a compilation error. Try compiling a small example: create Vehicle with a parameterized constructor and then create Car without calling super — you will see the compiler remind you to provide a proper constructor call. That experience reinforces how extends and constructor chaining work together.

keyIdea.title: extends usage
keyIdea.text: Use extends to create a subclass that inherits non-private members from a superclass and ensure proper constructor chaining.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Using the extends Keyword
Code Walkthrough

Vehicle and Car example

<!-- Vehicle.java -->
class Vehicle {
  String brand;
  int speed;

  public Vehicle(String brand) {
    this.brand = brand;
    this.speed = 0;
    System.out.println("Vehicle constructor called for " + brand);
  }

  public void start() {
    System.out.println(brand + " is starting.");
  }

  public void accelerate(int increment) {
    speed += increment;
    System.out.println(brand + " accelerating. Current speed: " + speed + " mph.");
  }
}

<!-- Car.java -->
class Car extends Vehicle {
  int numberOfDoors;

  public Car(String brand, int doors) {
    super(brand); // call to superclass constructor
    this.numberOfDoors = doors;
  }

  public void honk() {
    System.out.println("Beep beep!");
  }
}
• Car extends Vehicle so Car instances have brand, speed, start and accelerate available.
• The Car constructor calls super(brand) to initialize the Vehicle state.
• If Vehicle had no no-argument constructor, omitting super(...) in Car causes a compile error.
Practical notes

Remember that extends changes type relationships. A method accepting a Vehicle can accept a Car because Car is a Vehicle.

Common mistake

Forgetting to call a required superclass constructor is a frequent compile-time error when the superclass lacks a no-argument constructor.

Check your understanding

Try creating Vehicle with only a parameterized constructor, then make a Car and see the compiler message if you omit super(...).

screens.title: Superclass and Subclass: What Is Inherited?
screens.subtitle: Which members flow down the inheritance chain and which remain hidden

narration.text: A subclass automatically gains access to all non-private members of its superclass: that includes public and protected fields and methods and package-private members when in the same package. However, private members are inherited in the sense that they are part of the object's memory layout, but they are not directly accessible to the subclass; access must occur through the superclass's public or protected methods. For example, if Vehicle has a private field engineSerial and a public getEngineSerial method, Car can call getEngineSerial but cannot reference engineSerial directly. Protected is especially useful in inheritance because it allows subclasses in other packages to access the member while keeping it hidden from unrelated classes. This gives a balanced encapsulation model: internal details can be shared with subclasses without opening them to the whole world. A common misconception is assuming protected means global access — it does not. Another pitfall is trying to override private methods: since private methods cannot be seen by subclasses, declaring a method with the same signature creates an independent method rather than an override. Key takeaway: design your superclass A P I deliberately so subclasses can reuse behavior through protected or public members, while keeping truly internal details private.

keyIdea.title: Inheritance visibility
keyIdea.text: Public and protected members are accessible in subclasses; private members are inherited but not directly accessible.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Superclass and Subclass: What Is Inherited?
Hierarchy

Which members are available to subclasses?

• public members: always accessible to subclasses and other classes.
• protected members: accessible to subclasses even in different packages.
• package-private members: accessible when subclass is in the same package.
• private members: part of the class but not directly accessible to subclasses.
Concrete example

If Vehicle has private engineSerial and public getEngineSerial(), Car should call getEngineSerial() rather than attempting to read engineSerial directly.

Design guidance

Use protected sparingly for members that are intended to be extended by subclasses. Keep truly internal details private and expose behavior via protected or public methods.

Common mistake

Attempting to override a private method leads to an independent method in the subclass, not an override. Use @Override to detect such errors.

Key Takeaway

Control visibility intentionally: protected for subclass collaboration, private for strict encapsulation, public for API exposure.

screens.title: Method Overriding vs Method Overloading
screens.subtitle: Clear differences and how to recognize each case

narration.text: Method overriding and method overloading are often confused but they are distinct concepts. Overriding happens when a subclass provides a new implementation for a method with exactly the same signature as the superclass. This enables polymorphism: when you call that method on a reference typed as the superclass, the runtime selects the subclass implementation. For example, Car overrides start() to implement Car-specific startup behavior while preserving the same name and parameters. By contrast, overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class or across a hierarchy; it provides different ways to call a method depending on argument types and counts. A common error is changing parameters when intending to override, which results in overloading or compilation confusion rather than polymorphic behavior. Use @Override on overridden methods; it alerts the compiler if your signature does not match the superclass and prevents accidental overloading. Concrete example: if Vehicle has public void start(), declaring public void start(String mode) in Car is overloading, not overriding. Closing takeaway: check your method signatures and apply @Override to make your intent explicit.

keyIdea.title: Override vs Overload
keyIdea.text: Overriding keeps the same signature to change behavior; overloading changes parameters to offer multiple call forms.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Method Overriding vs Method Overloading
Comparison

Same name, different meaning

• Overriding: same signature in subclass; changes behavior; supports polymorphism.
• Overloading: same name, different parameters; multiple method forms in the same class or hierarchy.
• Use @Override to ensure you are overriding, not unintentionally overloading.
Example

Vehicle: public void start(); Car: @Override public void start() — this is overriding. Car: public void start(String mode) — this is overloading.

Misconception

Changing parameters when you intended to override prevents polymorphic behavior and can hide bugs. Rely on @Override to avoid this mistake.

Check

Look at a pair of methods with the same name. Ask: are their parameter lists identical? If yes and they are in superclass/subclass, this is overriding.

screens.title: The @Override Annotation
screens.subtitle: How the compiler helps you avoid signature errors

narration.text: The @Override annotation is an optional but highly recommended compiler directive that makes your intention explicit: you mean to override a superclass method. When you place @Override above a method, the compiler checks that a matching method exists in the superclass. If the signature does not match, the compiler raises an error. This avoids subtle bugs where you think you overrode a method but actually created a new unrelated method due to a typo or parameter mismatch. For example, if Vehicle defines public void start(), and you type @Override public void start(int delay), the compiler will flag a mismatch and force you to correct your signature. Another useful scenario is refactoring: if the superclass changes the method signature, @Override signals all subclasses that need adjustment. Common misconception: some developers believe @Override changes runtime behavior — it does not. It only enables compile-time checks. Key takeaway: use @Override on every overridden method to make your code safer and more maintainable. The @Override Annotation means annotate overridden methods to let the compiler verify that your signature matches the superclass implementation.. In practical terms, how the compiler helps you avoid signature errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: @Override purpose
keyIdea.text: Annotate overridden methods to let the compiler verify that your signature matches the superclass implementation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › The @Override Annotation
Definition

Let the compiler check your intent

@Override is a signal to the compiler that you intend to override a superclass method. If the signatures don't match, compilation fails so you can fix it immediately.

class Vehicle {
  public void start() {}
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
  @Override
  public void start() {
    // correct override
  }

  // Mistake: different parameters -> compiler flags if @Override is present
  // @Override
  // public void start(int delay) { }
}
Why it matters

It prevents accidental overloading when you intended overriding, and it aids safe refactoring of superclass methods.

Misconception

@Override does not alter runtime dispatch; it only performs compile-time verification of your signature intent.

screens.title: Calling super() in Constructors
screens.subtitle: How constructor chaining initializes the inherited part of an object

narration.text: Constructor chaining is the process where subclass constructors invoke superclass constructors to ensure the entire object is properly initialized. In Java, a call to a superclass constructor using super(...) must be the first statement in a subclass constructor. If you don't write super(...), the compiler inserts a no-argument super() call automatically. This behavior means that when a superclass only defines parameterized constructors and no no-argument constructor exists, you must explicitly call one of the superclass constructors from each subclass constructor. Consider Vehicle with public Vehicle(String brand). Car's constructor must call super(brand) as its first statement; otherwise compilation fails. A simple diagnostic exercise is to remove super from Car when Vehicle has no default constructor and observe the compiler error — it clearly points to missing constructor chaining. Another practical point: constructor calls flow from the most derived class up to Object, ensuring each level has a chance to initialize its part of the object. A common misconception is that super() can appear later in the constructor — it cannot. Key takeaway: always ensure subclass constructors perform the required superclass constructor call at the start so instances are correctly initialized.

keyIdea.title: Constructor chaining
keyIdea.text: super(...) must be the first statement in a subclass constructor to initialize the superclass portion of the object.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Calling super() in Constructors
Step-by-step

Constructor chaining rules

1) If you write super(...), it must be the first statement in the subclass constructor.
2) If you omit it, Java inserts a no-argument super() automatically.
3) If the superclass has only parameterized constructors, you must explicitly call one from the subclass.
class Vehicle {
  public Vehicle(String brand) { /* ... */ }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
  public Car(String brand, int doors) {
    super(brand); // required: superclass has no no-arg constructor
    this.numberOfDoors = doors;
  }
}
Common error

Omitting the required super(...) when the superclass lacks a default constructor triggers a compile-time error. Fix by adding the explicit call.

Check your understanding

Try removing super(...) from a subclass whose superclass only has parameterized constructors and observe the compiler message. Adjust constructors accordingly.

screens.title: Using super.method() from an Overridden Method
screens.subtitle: How to combine superclass behavior with subclass additions

narration.text: There are times when a subclass wants to extend the behavior of a superclass method rather than fully replace it. In those cases, you can call super. methodName() inside the overridden method to invoke the original implementation. For example, suppose Vehicle. start() performs essential initialization and Car wants to add Car-specific steps but still run the Vehicle startup. Car can override start(), call super. start() first to run the shared setup, and then perform its own actions like logging or car-specific startup. This pattern avoids duplicating the superclass logic and preserves centralized behavior. A common misconception is thinking super. method() bypasses polymorphism — it calls the immediate superclass implementation as written, which is precisely what you want when you need that behavior. Another pitfall is forgetting to maintain the same signature; if the signature changes, you no longer override and cannot call the superclass method polymorphically. Key takeaway: use super. method() to reuse superclass behavior and then add specialized logic in the subclass. Try writing an override that calls super and then performs extra steps. Using super.method() from an Overridden Method means call super.methodname() inside an overridden method to reuse superclass behavior then add subclass-specific logic.. In practical terms, how to combine superclass behavior with subclass additions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: super.method
keyIdea.text: Call super.methodName() inside an overridden method to reuse superclass behavior then add subclass-specific logic.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Using super.method() from an Overridden Method
Code Walkthrough

Extend, don't replace

class Vehicle {
  public void start() {
    System.out.println(brand + " is starting.");
    // common initialization
  }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
  @Override
  public void start() {
    super.start(); // run Vehicle startup logic
    System.out.println("Car " + brand + " is starting with a key.");
    // Car-specific startup
  }
}
• super.start() calls the immediate superclass implementation, preserving shared setup.
• Use this when subclass needs to add steps without duplicating superclass code.
Why it matters

It keeps initialization logic centralized while letting subclasses adapt behavior safely.

Misconception

super.method() calls the superclass version directly. It does not trigger dynamic dispatch to overridden methods further up the hierarchy in unexpected ways.

screens.title: Access Modifiers in Inheritance
screens.subtitle: Public, protected, package-private, and private in practice

narration.text: Access modifiers determine how superclass members are visible to subclasses. Public members are fully accessible everywhere. Protected members are accessible to subclasses even when those subclasses live in a different package, giving a controlled form of visibility useful for inheritance. Package-private (no modifier) is visible within the same package but not across package boundaries. Private members are intentionally hidden: a subclass inherits them as part of the object state, but it cannot reference them directly. A practical example: if you want subclasses to manipulate an internal field but prevent unrelated classes from doing so, consider protected accessor methods or protected fields. However, overusing protected fields can expose implementation details that make future refactors harder. A common novice mistake is altering private superclass state directly in a subclass; instead provide protected or public methods to perform controlled updates. Key takeaway: pick the least permissive modifier that supports intended subclass behavior, relying on protected for subclass collaboration and private when strict encapsulation is needed. Access Modifiers in Inheritance means choose the minimal visibility required for subclass interaction: protected for subclass use, private for strict encapsulation, public for api exposure.. In practical terms, public, protected, package-private, and private in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Access control
keyIdea.text: Choose the minimal visibility required for subclass interaction: protected for subclass use, private for strict encapsulation, public for API exposure.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Access Modifiers in Inheritance
Definition

Modifiers and their reach

• public: accessible to all classes, including subclasses.
• protected: accessible to subclasses across packages and within the same package.
• package-private: accessible only inside the same package.
• private: inaccessible directly to subclasses; access via public/protected methods only.
Design tip

Prefer methods that encapsulate state changes rather than exposing fields directly to subclasses. This keeps the superclass free to change implementation details later.

Concrete scenario

Vehicle exposes protected speed so subclasses can adjust it. The engineSerial stays private and is exposed via a public getter if needed.

Misconception

Protected is not a global access flag—it's targeted to subclasses and same-package classes only.

screens.title: Hands-on: Shape, Circle, Rectangle
screens.subtitle: Implement the Shape hierarchy and override calculateArea()

narration.text: This hands-on activity guides you through building a small inheritance hierarchy that exercises extends, super, and overriding. Start by creating a Shape superclass with a String color, a constructor that sets color, a displayColor() method, and a calculateArea() method that returns 0.0. Then create Circle and Rectangle that extend Shape. Circle adds radius and its constructor must call super(color). Override calculateArea() in Circle to return Math. PI * radius * radius. Rectangle adds length and width, calls super(color) in its constructor, and overrides calculateArea() to return length * width. Each subclass should also implement a displayDetails() method that calls displayColor() and prints its dimensions and area. Running the example demonstrates which overridden implementations execute. A common misconception to watch for is forgetting to call super(color) in each subclass constructor; if Shape has no no-argument constructor, the code won't compile. This small project checks many inheritance concepts at once: proper use of extends, constructor chaining, overriding, and calling superclass methods from subclasses. After implementing, run your main method and observe the sequence of constructor messages and which calculateArea implementation returns the correct values.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Build Shape→Circle/Rectangle to practice extends, constructor chaining via super, and overriding calculateArea.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Hands-on: Shape, Circle, Rectangle
Starter code
// Shape.java
class Shape {
  String color;

  public Shape(String color) {
    this.color = color;
  }

  public void displayColor() {
    System.out.println("Shape color: " + color);
  }

  public double calculateArea() {
    System.out.println("Calculating area for a generic shape.");
    return 0.0;
  }
}

// Circle.java
class Circle extends Shape {
  double radius;

  public Circle(String color, double radius) {
    super(color);
    this.radius = radius;
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateArea() {
    return Math.PI * radius * radius;
  }

  public void displayDetails() {
    displayColor();
    System.out.println("Radius: " + radius);
    System.out.println("Area: " + calculateArea());
  }
}

// Rectangle.java
class Rectangle extends Shape {
  double length;
  double width;

  public Rectangle(String color, double length, double width) {
    super(color);
    this.length = length;
    this.width = width;
  }

  @Override
  public double calculateArea() {
    return length * width;
  }

  public void displayDetails() {
    displayColor();
    System.out.println("Length: " + length + ", Width: " + width);
    System.out.println("Area: " + calculateArea());
  }
}
What to observe

When you instantiate Circle and call displayDetails(), the Circle.calculateArea() runs, not the Shape default. Constructors show super being called first.

Try this

Remove super(color) and compile to see the error when Shape has no default constructor. Then restore it to fix the code.

screens.title: Pitfalls and Debugging Tips
screens.subtitle: Common errors with inheritance and how to fix them

narration.text: Beginners commonly encounter a handful of recurring issues when using inheritance. First, forgetting to call an appropriate superclass constructor leads to a compile-time error when the superclass lacks a no-argument constructor. The fix is explicit super(...) as the first statement. Second, trying to override a private method creates a new method in the subclass rather than overriding; add @Override and switch to protected/public methods if you genuinely need to customize behavior. Third, accidentally changing a method signature when you intended to override results in overloading; use @Override to catch this early. Fourth, overexposing fields as protected can couple subclasses to implementation details and make refactoring harder; prefer protected or public accessor methods instead of direct field access. When debugging these issues, read compiler messages carefully: they often point to missing constructors or signature mismatches. Reproducing the error in a small test case helps isolate the problem. Key takeaway: rely on explicit constructor calls, use @Override, and prefer methods over direct field exposure to keep hierarchies robust and maintainable. Pitfalls and Debugging Tips means use explicit super calls, @override, and controlled access to avoid common inheritance bugs.. In practical terms, common errors with inheritance and how to fix them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debugging rules
keyIdea.text: Use explicit super calls, @Override, and controlled access to avoid common inheritance bugs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Pitfalls and Debugging Tips
Mistake

Missing super()

If the superclass defines only parameterized constructors, the subclass must call one explicitly as the first statement.

Mistake

Unintended overloading

Changing parameters when aiming to override creates a new method. Use @Override to detect this mistake early.

Mistake

Overexposing fields

Making fields protected ties subclasses to implementation. Prefer accessor methods for safer evolution.

Debugging tip

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Six compact reminders to guide correct inheritance use

narration.text: Finish with six concise reminders. First, method overriding requires an identical signature; use @Override to confirm your intent. Second, super allows you to call the superclass constructor or methods when you need the original behavior. Third, protected gives subclasses access even across packages but is not global access; choose it only when necessary. Fourth, private members are not directly accessible by subclasses and cannot be overridden. Fifth, constructor chaining always moves from subclass to superclass and requires super(...) as the first statement if used. Sixth, test small examples and read compiler messages closely — they reveal missing constructor calls or signature mismatches quickly. Keep these rules in mind as you design hierarchies and write exercises. A quick reflection question: which two reminders feel most likely to prevent bugs in your next Java class design?
